sections.title: Physics
paragraphs: Aurvantis behaves the way any traveler would expect: things fall, fires burn, and the sky holds one sun and two moons in steady orbit. Its native magnetism is weak enough that compasses drift near iron-rich ranges, which is why most seafaring peoples still swear by lodestone charts checked against the stars rather than the needle alone.
Motion and force follow the plain rules every blacksmith and shipwright already assumes; there is no recorded case of a catapult or a keel behaving other than expected.
The world's magnetic field is faint and irregular near volcanic ranges such as Drossakar's iron belt, enough to throw off an uncorrected compass but never enough to be dangerous on its own.

No scholar on Aurvantis works at a scale where such questions arise; alchemy is taught and practiced as the interaction of four classical elements, and it works well enough that nobody has pushed further.

sections.title: Cosmology
paragraphs: One sun, two moons — Aurel, which is quick and pale, and Vantis, which is slow and copper-dark — light a single world-ocean broken by four continents: forested Kelmoria, volcanic Drossakar, arid Sunkeep Reaches, and the tropical Veyl Isles. Each continent's peoples read the moons' opposed cycles differently, which is the single largest source of calendar disputes at any international gathering.

No creation account is treated as more true than any other; Kelmorian elves tell of a world sung into being, Drossakar orc-clans of a world hammered out of chaos-slag, and no priesthood has ever produced proof sufficient to settle it.

Aurel completes its circuit in twenty-nine days, Vantis in sixty-one; their rare joint alignment, the Doubling, is treated as an omen year across nearly every calendar on the world regardless of faith.

The First World, home of the fey, sits close enough to Aurvantis that certain groves, sea-caves, and standing stones serve as crossing points; these are rare, well-mapped, and universally treated with caution.

sections.title: Magic
paragraphs: Magic on Aurvantis draws on an ambient field called the Veil, strongest along coastlines and mountain spines, which is why so many nations' capitals sit on one or the other. Arcane casters draw the current directly, divine casters channel it through a deity's grant, and a scattering of bloodline talents — sorcerers, oracles, and the like — simply carry an inherited thread of it.

Three traditions coexist without much friction: arcane study (drawing raw current through learned formulae), divine grant (channeling a deity's portion of the Veil through faith and ritual), and primal or bloodline talent (an inherited thread of current that manifests without formal training).

A working large enough to reshape terrain or move an army draws down the local Veil for months, leaving the area's minor magic — cantrips, minor healing, wardings — measurably weaker until it replenishes.
The Veil pools most densely where land meets open water or high altitude, which is why Sunkeep's high aeries and Veyl's reef-cities both produce disproportionate numbers of capable casters.

Current drawn faster than it replenishes curdles into a wild zone: a patch of ground where spells misfire, water runs the wrong temperature, and nothing sensible builds a permanent structure. Every continent has at least one, usually fenced off and mapped by whichever nation is nearest.

sections.title: Metaphysics
paragraphs: Gods are widely believed real and are occasionally, verifiably active through their clergy's granted power, but none claims the whole world's worship, and none intervenes directly often enough to settle any theological argument for good.
Clergy across every continent can point to real, testable divine grants — healing, wards, restored sight — which keeps temples relevant even where formal belief has eroded into habit.

sections.title: Technology
paragraphs: Iron and steel carry Aurvantis's armies and its plows alike; enchantment exists but is slow, expensive, and mostly reserved for a nation's standing military or its wealthiest guilds.

Ordinary iron and steel are available everywhere ore and fuel meet; enchanted alloys — cold-worked mithral in Sunkeep's deep holds, coral-forged bronze in the Veyl Isles — are rare enough to be a mark of status wherever they turn up.
No continent has fielded anything resembling gunpowder at scale; siege warfare runs on torsion engines, alchemical fire, and — where a nation can afford it — battle magic.

sections.title: Geography
paragraphs: Drossakar is defined by ash-fields, iron-rich badlands, geothermal vents — a landscape that shaped every nation built on it long before any of their current borders existed. Volcanic ridgelines, black-rock canyons, a few fertile crater basins sets the pattern of where people actually settled, and the climate — hot, dry, prone to ashfall storms off the active peaks — decided what they could grow, mine, or hunt once they did.

The mix of ash-fields, iron-rich badlands, geothermal vents on Drossakar means no single nation here can rely on one kind of land; every nation's economy blends what each biome offers rather than specializing in just one.

Volcanic ridgelines, black-rock canyons, a few fertile crater basins across Drossakar has kept its four nations more separated by geography than by any deliberate border policy — most conflicts here start at a natural chokepoint, not an arbitrary line.

A hot, dry, prone to ashfall storms off the active peaks climate governs the planting, trading, and travel calendar for every nation on Drossakar, and every one of them has built its major festivals around it.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Drossakar has been settled continuously since before the Doubling of Founding, first by scattered clans of its founding peoples and later by the four organized nations that now hold it. The Veil-Storms of -410 reshaped its coastline and interior alike, and the Long Peace Accords of 112 are still the framework every nation here formally honors, however unevenly.
Histories on Drossakar are conventionally divided into the Founding Era (before -410), the unstable Veil-Storm centuries that followed, and the Long Peace that has held, roughly, since 112.
The Veil-Storms remain the single most-referenced disaster in every nation's oldest records on Drossakar, blamed for everything from reshaped coastlines to the continent's scattered wild zones.

Population on Drossakar has drifted steadily toward its rivers, coasts, and trade roads for generations, hollowing out its more remote interior settlements in favor of its four nations' capitals and market towns.

sections.title: Demographics
paragraphs: Drossakar is home to the Orc, Half-Orc, Hobgoblin, Goblin peoples, each concentrated in its own nation but present as trading minorities nearly everywhere else on the continent.
Orc, Half-Orc, Hobgoblin, Goblin together make up the overwhelming majority of Drossakar's population, with small numbers of other Aurvantan peoples present in every major port and market town.
Movement across Drossakar runs mostly along its trade roads and river lines rather than across open wilderness, which keeps its nations' borders porous for merchants even when politically tense.
Drossakar supports a population in the low millions, weighted heavily toward its four national capitals and the market towns strung along the routes between them.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Ashgate Reach is governed by an elected assembly of company-captains, an arrangement that grew directly out of how Half-Orc settlers on Drossakar organized themselves in the generations after the Doubling of Founding. It has held largely unchanged since, adjusted at the margins but never formally overthrown.

Law in Ashgate Reach is set and interpreted by an elected assembly of company-captains, with each of the nation's four cities left to handle enforcement details locally so long as they don't contradict the nation's core code.
Authority in Ashgate Reach flows downward from an elected assembly of company-captains to each city's local ruler, who in turn answers for their city's conduct at the nation's periodic councils.

Ashgate Reach relies on city militias for day-to-day order, backed by standing patrols along its more contested borders — a compromise that keeps costs down but leaves remote stretches thinly watched.

sections.title: Identity
paragraphs: Ashgate Reach is a Half-Orc-majority nation on Drossakar, and its laws, holidays, and public architecture all reflect Half-Orc custom even where other peoples make up a sizable minority of its population.

Ashgate Reach's stated priorities are preserving its autonomy, keeping its trade routes secure, and honoring the Long Peace Accords — though in practice the first two frequently take precedence over the third when they conflict.

Ashgate Reach occupies territory on Drossakar that its people have held since before the Long Peace, giving its claim to the land a legitimacy few neighbors formally dispute, whatever they say in private.
Ashgate Reach maintains formal ties with its neighbors on Drossakar and trade contacts reaching all three other continents, conducted mostly through its merchant houses rather than formal embassies.

sections.title: Economy
paragraphs: Ashgate Reach's economy runs on mercenary contracts and tempered steel, produced and traded through its four principal cities and shaping nearly every other aspect of its politics, from tax policy to who holds real influence in an elected assembly of company-captains.

Ashgate Reach produces mercenary contracts and tempered steel in quantities enough to export widely, a trade that has made certain families and guilds within the nation disproportionately wealthy and influential.

Ashgate Reach exports mercenary contracts and tempered steel through its four principal cities, trading them for goods its own land and craft cannot supply — a dependency that keeps its merchant houses politically powerful.

Labor in Ashgate Reach splits between guild-apprenticed craft work in its cities and traditional household or clan labor in its more rural stretches, with real tension between the two systems over status and pay.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Ashgate Reach was founded in the generations following the Doubling of Founding by Half-Orc settlers on Drossakar, consolidating slowly from scattered early settlements into the nation recognized today.

Ashgate Reach's founding myths center on the Doubling of Founding and the nation's first recognized leader, whose exact deeds vary considerably depending on which city's version of the story is being told.
Ashgate Reach consolidated gradually from a scatter of early settlements into its current four principal cities, a process that took generations and was never fully peaceful.

Ashgate Reach's most persistent internal conflict centers on a border shrine both sides claim, a dispute old enough that few remember exactly how it started but recent enough that it still shapes local politics.

sections.title: Factions
paragraphs: A faction within Ashgate Reach actively contests smuggling routes, organizing support in whichever of the nation's cities gives it the most leverage.
This faction's central aim is control over a disputed succession, pursued through both legitimate political pressure and, when that fails, quieter means.
Its influence is concentrated in one or two of Ashgate Reach's four cities rather than spread evenly across the nation, which is exactly why the formal government has been slow to move against it.
An elected assembly of company-captains remains this faction's chief opponent, treating it as a persistent irritant rather than an existential threat — a judgment that may not age well.

As a result, its founding compromise is still cited in local law, a legacy every resident of Harforge would recognize immediately even if outsiders rarely do.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Cinderwarren is governed by a chieftain-swarm where authority shifts with demonstrated cunning, an arrangement that grew directly out of how Goblin settlers on Drossakar organized themselves in the generations after the Doubling of Founding. It has held largely unchanged since, adjusted at the margins but never formally overthrown.

Law in Cinderwarren is set and interpreted by a chieftain-swarm where authority shifts with demonstrated cunning, with each of the nation's four cities left to handle enforcement details locally so long as they don't contradict the nation's core code.

Authority in Cinderwarren flows downward from a chieftain-swarm where authority shifts with demonstrated cunning to each city's local ruler, who in turn answers for their city's conduct at the nation's periodic councils.
Cinderwarren relies on city militias for day-to-day order, backed by standing patrols along its more contested borders — a compromise that keeps costs down but leaves remote stretches thinly watched.

sections.title: Identity
paragraphs: Cinderwarren is a Goblin-majority nation on Drossakar, and its laws, holidays, and public architecture all reflect Goblin custom even where other peoples make up a sizable minority of its population.

Cinderwarren's stated priorities are preserving its autonomy, keeping its trade routes secure, and honoring the Long Peace Accords — though in practice the first two frequently take precedence over the third when they conflict.

Cinderwarren occupies territory on Drossakar that its people have held since before the Long Peace, giving its claim to the land a legitimacy few neighbors formally dispute, whatever they say in private.
Cinderwarren maintains formal ties with its neighbors on Drossakar and trade contacts reaching all three other continents, conducted mostly through its merchant houses rather than formal embassies.

sections.title: Economy
paragraphs: Cinderwarren's economy runs on salvage, fungus cultivation, and alchemical explosives, produced and traded through its four principal cities and shaping nearly every other aspect of its politics, from tax policy to who holds real influence in a chieftain-swarm where authority shifts with demonstrated cunning.

Cinderwarren produces salvage, fungus cultivation, and alchemical explosives in quantities enough to export widely, a trade that has made certain families and guilds within the nation disproportionately wealthy and influential.

Cinderwarren exports salvage, fungus cultivation, and alchemical explosives through its four principal cities, trading them for goods its own land and craft cannot supply — a dependency that keeps its merchant houses politically powerful.

Labor in Cinderwarren splits between guild-apprenticed craft work in its cities and traditional household or clan labor in its more rural stretches, with real tension between the two systems over status and pay.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Cinderwarren was founded in the generations following the Doubling of Founding by Goblin settlers on Drossakar, consolidating slowly from scattered early settlements into the nation recognized today.

Cinderwarren's founding myths center on the Doubling of Founding and the nation's first recognized leader, whose exact deeds vary considerably depending on which city's version of the story is being told.
Cinderwarren consolidated gradually from a scatter of early settlements into its current four principal cities, a process that took generations and was never fully peaceful.

Cinderwarren's most persistent internal conflict centers on an old unpaid blood-debt, a dispute old enough that few remember exactly how it started but recent enough that it still shapes local politics.

sections.title: Factions
paragraphs: A faction within Cinderwarren actively contests control of a trade toll, organizing support in whichever of the nation's cities gives it the most leverage.
This faction's central aim is control over a heretical splinter cult, pursued through both legitimate political pressure and, when that fails, quieter means.
Its influence is concentrated in one or two of Cinderwarren's four cities rather than spread evenly across the nation, which is exactly why the formal government has been slow to move against it.

A chieftain-swarm where authority shifts with demonstrated cunning remains this faction's chief opponent, treating it as a persistent irritant rather than an existential threat — a judgment that may not age well.

The root of Cinderheap's trouble is a border shrine both sides claim, a dispute old enough that most residents have simply learned to live around it.

sections.title: History

Cinderheap was founded by early Goblin settlers of Cinderwarren, drawn to the site by exactly the resources that still support the city's trade.
In its history, Cinderheap grew rich off a single trade good before diversifying, an event still referenced in local memory and civic ritual.
As a result, its founding compromise is still cited in local law, a legacy every resident of Cinderheap would recognize immediately even if outsiders rarely do.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Ironjaw Legion is governed by a military bureaucracy organized entirely by rank, an arrangement that grew directly out of how Hobgoblin settlers on Drossakar organized themselves in the generations after the Doubling of Founding. It has held largely unchanged since, adjusted at the margins but never formally overthrown.

Law in Ironjaw Legion is set and interpreted by a military bureaucracy organized entirely by rank, with each of the nation's four cities left to handle enforcement details locally so long as they don't contradict the nation's core code.

Authority in Ironjaw Legion flows downward from a military bureaucracy organized entirely by rank to each city's local ruler, who in turn answers for their city's conduct at the nation's periodic councils.

Ironjaw Legion relies on city militias for day-to-day order, backed by standing patrols along its more contested borders — a compromise that keeps costs down but leaves remote stretches thinly watched.

sections.title: Identity
paragraphs: Ironjaw Legion is a Hobgoblin-majority nation on Drossakar, and its laws, holidays, and public architecture all reflect Hobgoblin custom even where other peoples make up a sizable minority of its population.

Ironjaw Legion's stated priorities are preserving its autonomy, keeping its trade routes secure, and honoring the Long Peace Accords — though in practice the first two frequently take precedence over the third when they conflict.

Ironjaw Legion occupies territory on Drossakar that its people have held since before the Long Peace, giving its claim to the land a legitimacy few neighbors formally dispute, whatever they say in private.
Ironjaw Legion maintains formal ties with its neighbors on Drossakar and trade contacts reaching all three other continents, conducted mostly through its merchant houses rather than formal embassies.

sections.title: Economy
paragraphs: Ironjaw Legion's economy runs on weapons manufacture and logistics contracting, produced and traded through its four principal cities and shaping nearly every other aspect of its politics, from tax policy to who holds real influence in a military bureaucracy organized entirely by rank.

Ironjaw Legion produces weapons manufacture and logistics contracting in quantities enough to export widely, a trade that has made certain families and guilds within the nation disproportionately wealthy and influential.

Ironjaw Legion exports weapons manufacture and logistics contracting through its four principal cities, trading them for goods its own land and craft cannot supply — a dependency that keeps its merchant houses politically powerful.

Labor in Ironjaw Legion splits between guild-apprenticed craft work in its cities and traditional household or clan labor in its more rural stretches, with real tension between the two systems over status and pay.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Ironjaw Legion was founded in the generations following the Doubling of Founding by Hobgoblin settlers on Drossakar, consolidating slowly from scattered early settlements into the nation recognized today.

Ironjaw Legion's founding myths center on the Doubling of Founding and the nation's first recognized leader, whose exact deeds vary considerably depending on which city's version of the story is being told.
Ironjaw Legion consolidated gradually from a scatter of early settlements into its current four principal cities, a process that took generations and was never fully peaceful.

Ironjaw Legion's most persistent internal conflict centers on a border shrine both sides claim, a dispute old enough that few remember exactly how it started but recent enough that it still shapes local politics.

sections.title: Factions
paragraphs: A faction within Ironjaw Legion actively contests grazing land, organizing support in whichever of the nation's cities gives it the most leverage.
This faction's central aim is control over an old unpaid blood-debt, pursued through both legitimate political pressure and, when that fails, quieter means.
Its influence is concentrated in one or two of Ironjaw Legion's four cities rather than spread evenly across the nation, which is exactly why the formal government has been slow to move against it.
A military bureaucracy organized entirely by rank remains this faction's chief opponent, treating it as a persistent irritant rather than an existential threat — a judgment that may not age well.

sections.title: Urban Life
paragraphs: Ironguard runs on a landed gentry above a tenant-farming majority, a structure visible in everything from who sits closest to the reeve at public gatherings to who gets first pick of goods at market.
Status in Ironguard runs on a landed gentry above a tenant-farming majority, a system locals mostly accept as fair and outsiders mostly find baffling.
Ironguard's daily rhythm is set by mandatory tithe-days each new moon, observed closely enough that a stranger who ignores it draws immediate notice.
Ironguard is built from salt-washed adobe with flat roofs for drying goods, a style shaped directly by Drossakar's climate and the materials its Hobgoblin founders had on hand.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Ironguard answers upward to Ironjaw Legion, governed by a military bureaucracy organized entirely by rank, though in practice its local rulers exercise considerable day-to-day discretion so long as tribute and trade flow as expected.
Formal authority in Ironguard rests with a local reeve, confirmed by Ironjaw Legion's central government but drawn, by long custom, from the city's own leading families.
Beneath the formal government, a black-market alchemist collective exercises real influence in Ironguard — acknowledged quietly by everyone who actually has to get business done there.

Day-to-day administration in Ironguard runs through clan-appointed reeves who answer to their own elders first, a system that works well enough in ordinary times but strains badly under any real crisis.

sections.title: Tension
paragraphs: Ironguard's deepest ongoing friction is over a heretical splinter cult, a dispute that shapes local politics more than any formal law does.
Tension in Ironguard currently sits at a simmer — real, openly discussed, but not yet at open conflict.
The root of Ironguard's trouble is a heretical splinter cult, a dispute old enough that most residents have simply learned to live around it.
Ironguard rarely sees real violence over this, but trade disputes have been known to bring things close to a boil, especially during the busy trading season.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Ironguard was settled by Hobgoblin migrants and grew into its current standing as a town on the strength of its trade in logistics contracting, which remains the backbone of its economy today.
Ironguard was founded by early Hobgoblin settlers of Ironjaw Legion, drawn to the site by exactly the resources that still support the city's trade.
In its history, Ironguard was founded explicitly to guard a mountain pass or river ford, an event still referenced in local memory and civic ritual.
As a result, it is now the region's acknowledged center of learning, a legacy every resident of Ironguard would recognize immediately even if outsiders rarely do.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Kragmoor Horde is governed by a warlord's retinue confirmed by trial of combat every decade, an arrangement that grew directly out of how Orc settlers on Drossakar organized themselves in the generations after the Doubling of Founding. It has held largely unchanged since, adjusted at the margins but never formally overthrown.

Law in Kragmoor Horde is set and interpreted by a warlord's retinue confirmed by trial of combat every decade, with each of the nation's four cities left to handle enforcement details locally so long as they don't contradict the nation's core code.

Authority in Kragmoor Horde flows downward from a warlord's retinue confirmed by trial of combat every decade to each city's local ruler, who in turn answers for their city's conduct at the nation's periodic councils.

Kragmoor Horde relies on city militias for day-to-day order, backed by standing patrols along its more contested borders — a compromise that keeps costs down but leaves remote stretches thinly watched.

sections.title: Identity
paragraphs: Kragmoor Horde is a Orc-majority nation on Drossakar, and its laws, holidays, and public architecture all reflect Orc custom even where other peoples make up a sizable minority of its population.

Kragmoor Horde's stated priorities are preserving its autonomy, keeping its trade routes secure, and honoring the Long Peace Accords — though in practice the first two frequently take precedence over the third when they conflict.

Kragmoor Horde occupies territory on Drossakar that its people have held since before the Long Peace, giving its claim to the land a legitimacy few neighbors formally dispute, whatever they say in private.
Kragmoor Horde maintains formal ties with its neighbors on Drossakar and trade contacts reaching all three other continents, conducted mostly through its merchant houses rather than formal embassies.

sections.title: Economy
paragraphs: Kragmoor Horde's economy runs on iron, livestock, and mercenary muscle, produced and traded through its four principal cities and shaping nearly every other aspect of its politics, from tax policy to who holds real influence in a warlord's retinue confirmed by trial of combat every decade.

Kragmoor Horde produces iron, livestock, and mercenary muscle in quantities enough to export widely, a trade that has made certain families and guilds within the nation disproportionately wealthy and influential.

Kragmoor Horde exports iron, livestock, and mercenary muscle through its four principal cities, trading them for goods its own land and craft cannot supply — a dependency that keeps its merchant houses politically powerful.

Labor in Kragmoor Horde splits between guild-apprenticed craft work in its cities and traditional household or clan labor in its more rural stretches, with real tension between the two systems over status and pay.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Kragmoor Horde was founded in the generations following the Doubling of Founding by Orc settlers on Drossakar, consolidating slowly from scattered early settlements into the nation recognized today.

Kragmoor Horde's founding myths center on the Doubling of Founding and the nation's first recognized leader, whose exact deeds vary considerably depending on which city's version of the story is being told.
Kragmoor Horde consolidated gradually from a scatter of early settlements into its current four principal cities, a process that took generations and was never fully peaceful.

Kragmoor Horde's most persistent internal conflict centers on a heretical splinter cult, a dispute old enough that few remember exactly how it started but recent enough that it still shapes local politics.

sections.title: Factions
paragraphs: A faction within Kragmoor Horde actively contests water rights, organizing support in whichever of the nation's cities gives it the most leverage.
This faction's central aim is control over a disputed succession, pursued through both legitimate political pressure and, when that fails, quieter means.
Its influence is concentrated in one or two of Kragmoor Horde's four cities rather than spread evenly across the nation, which is exactly why the formal government has been slow to move against it.

A warlord's retinue confirmed by trial of combat every decade remains this faction's chief opponent, treating it as a persistent irritant rather than an existential threat — a judgment that may not age well.

sections.title: Urban Life
paragraphs: Kragmoor runs on a warrior caste ranked above artisans and laborers, a structure visible in everything from who sits closest to the reeve at public gatherings to who gets first pick of goods at market.
Status in Kragmoor runs on a warrior caste ranked above artisans and laborers, a system locals mostly accept as fair and outsiders mostly find baffling.
Kragmoor's daily rhythm is set by a weekly rest-day observed even by the guard, observed closely enough that a stranger who ignores it draws immediate notice.
Kragmoor is built from woven cane platforms strung between trees, a style shaped directly by Drossakar's climate and the materials its Orc founders had on hand.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Kragmoor answers upward to Kragmoor Horde, governed by a warlord's retinue confirmed by trial of combat every decade, though in practice its local rulers exercise considerable day-to-day discretion so long as tribute and trade flow as expected.
Formal authority in Kragmoor rests with a local reeve, confirmed by Kragmoor Horde's central government but drawn, by long custom, from the city's own leading families.
Beneath the formal government, an old veterans' league nobody in office will cross exercises real influence in Kragmoor — acknowledged quietly by everyone who actually has to get business done there.
Day-to-day administration in Kragmoor runs through rotating magistrates drawn by lot each season, a system that works well enough in ordinary times but strains badly under any real crisis.

sections.title: Tension
paragraphs: Kragmoor's deepest ongoing friction is over water rights, a dispute that shapes local politics more than any formal law does.
Tension in Kragmoor currently sits at a simmer — real, openly discussed, but not yet at open conflict.
The root of Kragmoor's trouble is water rights, a dispute old enough that most residents have simply learned to live around it.
Kragmoor rarely sees real violence over this, but trade disputes have been known to bring things close to a boil, especially during the busy trading season.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Kragmoor was settled by Orc migrants and grew into its current standing as a town on the strength of its trade in livestock, which remains the backbone of its economy today.
Kragmoor was founded by early Orc settlers of Kragmoor Horde, drawn to the site by exactly the resources that still support the city's trade.
In its history, Kragmoor split from a larger settlement after a succession dispute, an event still referenced in local memory and civic ritual.
As a result, its founding event is reenacted every year as a public festival, a legacy every resident of Kragmoor would recognize immediately even if outsiders rarely do.

paragraphs: Vormoor's deepest ongoing friction is over water rights, a dispute that shapes local politics more than any formal law does.

sections.title: History

sections.title: Geography
paragraphs: Kelmoria is defined by river-valley farmland, old-growth deciduous forest, rolling downs — a landscape that shaped every nation built on it long before any of their current borders existed. Gentle hills cut by three major rivers, thick forest along the western spine sets the pattern of where people actually settled, and the climate — temperate, four clear seasons, reliable rainfall — decided what they could grow, mine, or hunt once they did.

The mix of river-valley farmland, old-growth deciduous forest, rolling downs on Kelmoria means no single nation here can rely on one kind of land; every nation's economy blends what each biome offers rather than specializing in just one.

Gentle hills cut by three major rivers, thick forest along the western spine across Kelmoria has kept its four nations more separated by geography than by any deliberate border policy — most conflicts here start at a natural chokepoint, not an arbitrary line.

A temperate, four clear seasons, reliable rainfall climate governs the planting, trading, and travel calendar for every nation on Kelmoria, and every one of them has built its major festivals around it.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Kelmoria has been settled continuously since before the Doubling of Founding, first by scattered clans of its founding peoples and later by the four organized nations that now hold it. The Veil-Storms of -410 reshaped its coastline and interior alike, and the Long Peace Accords of 112 are still the framework every nation here formally honors, however unevenly.
Histories on Kelmoria are conventionally divided into the Founding Era (before -410), the unstable Veil-Storm centuries that followed, and the Long Peace that has held, roughly, since 112.
The Veil-Storms remain the single most-referenced disaster in every nation's oldest records on Kelmoria, blamed for everything from reshaped coastlines to the continent's scattered wild zones.

Population on Kelmoria has drifted steadily toward its rivers, coasts, and trade roads for generations, hollowing out its more remote interior settlements in favor of its four nations' capitals and market towns.

sections.title: Demographics
paragraphs: Kelmoria is home to the Human, Elf, Half-Elf, Gnome peoples, each concentrated in its own nation but present as trading minorities nearly everywhere else on the continent.
Human, Elf, Half-Elf, Gnome together make up the overwhelming majority of Kelmoria's population, with small numbers of other Aurvantan peoples present in every major port and market town.
Movement across Kelmoria runs mostly along its trade roads and river lines rather than across open wilderness, which keeps its nations' borders porous for merchants even when politically tense.
Kelmoria supports a population in the low millions, weighted heavily toward its four national capitals and the market towns strung along the routes between them.

sections.title: Origin
paragraphs: Elf trace their homeland to old-growth forest, tended more than owned, and even where they've spread across Aurvantis, that origin still shapes their architecture, diet, and holidays.

sections.title: Belief
paragraphs: Ancestor-reverence blended with reverence for the deep forest itself. This belief system underlies most Elf holidays, funeral rites, and everyday small courtesies.

Elf mark major life passages with rites tied to the local calendar and the twin-moon cycle, adjusted by every individual clan or household to their own circumstances.
Among Elf, oath-breaking and violations of hospitality are treated as near-universal wrongs, punished more by loss of standing than by any formal law.

sections.title: Society
paragraphs: Multi-generational households where the eldest living member holds final say. This structure determines who speaks for a family in a dispute and who inherits what when someone dies.

Among Elf, authority is earned more through demonstrated competence than pure inheritance, though a respected family name still opens doors a stranger doesn't get.
Status among Elf is legible through visible trade success, craft skill, and the debts and favors a person is owed, more than through formal title alone.

sections.title: Subsistence
paragraphs: Elf livelihoods are shaped directly by Kelmoria's river-valley farmland, old-growth deciduous forest, rolling downs, and their traditional trades reflect exactly what that land offers.
Most Elf make their living through farming, trade, or craft suited to Kelmoria's terrain, adapted over generations to work with the land rather than against it.
Elf craft goods are recognizable across Aurvantis by their distinctive materials and style, and command a premium in foreign markets specifically because of that origin.
Elf remain most heavily concentrated on Kelmoria, though small trading communities are found on every other continent as well.

sections.title: Relations
paragraphs: Elf maintain generally peaceful relations with their neighboring peoples on Kelmoria, punctuated by periodic disputes over resources or old, specific grievances.
Elf are represented, unevenly, in the nation of Kelmoria that shares their cultural roots most closely, and view that nation's government as at least nominally answerable to them.
Elf maintain both close kin-ties and long-standing rivalries with the other peoples of Kelmoria, the specifics varying from clan to clan and city to city.
Specific old grievances between Elf and their neighbors persist in local memory, but rarely rise to open conflict under the terms of the Long Peace.

sections.title: Belief
paragraphs: Frequently blends both parent cultures' practices, sometimes uneasily. This belief system underlies most Half-Elf holidays, funeral rites, and everyday small courtesies.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Ardenhale is governed by a hereditary court balanced by a chartered merchant assembly, an arrangement that grew directly out of how Human settlers on Kelmoria organized themselves in the generations after the Doubling of Founding. It has held largely unchanged since, adjusted at the margins but never formally overthrown.

Law in Ardenhale is set and interpreted by a hereditary court balanced by a chartered merchant assembly, with each of the nation's four cities left to handle enforcement details locally so long as they don't contradict the nation's core code.

Authority in Ardenhale flows downward from a hereditary court balanced by a chartered merchant assembly to each city's local ruler, who in turn answers for their city's conduct at the nation's periodic councils.
Ardenhale relies on city militias for day-to-day order, backed by standing patrols along its more contested borders — a compromise that keeps costs down but leaves remote stretches thinly watched.

sections.title: Identity
paragraphs: Ardenhale is a Human-majority nation on Kelmoria, and its laws, holidays, and public architecture all reflect Human custom even where other peoples make up a sizable minority of its population.

Ardenhale's stated priorities are preserving its autonomy, keeping its trade routes secure, and honoring the Long Peace Accords — though in practice the first two frequently take precedence over the third when they conflict.
Ardenhale occupies territory on Kelmoria that its people have held since before the Long Peace, giving its claim to the land a legitimacy few neighbors formally dispute, whatever they say in private.
Ardenhale maintains formal ties with its neighbors on Kelmoria and trade contacts reaching all three other continents, conducted mostly through its merchant houses rather than formal embassies.

sections.title: Economy
paragraphs: Ardenhale's economy runs on grain, timber, and river-borne trade goods, produced and traded through its four principal cities and shaping nearly every other aspect of its politics, from tax policy to who holds real influence in a hereditary court balanced by a chartered merchant assembly.

Ardenhale produces grain, timber, and river-borne trade goods in quantities enough to export widely, a trade that has made certain families and guilds within the nation disproportionately wealthy and influential.

Ardenhale exports grain, timber, and river-borne trade goods through its four principal cities, trading them for goods its own land and craft cannot supply — a dependency that keeps its merchant houses politically powerful.

Labor in Ardenhale splits between guild-apprenticed craft work in its cities and traditional household or clan labor in its more rural stretches, with real tension between the two systems over status and pay.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Ardenhale was founded in the generations following the Doubling of Founding by Human settlers on Kelmoria, consolidating slowly from scattered early settlements into the nation recognized today.

Ardenhale's founding myths center on the Doubling of Founding and the nation's first recognized leader, whose exact deeds vary considerably depending on which city's version of the story is being told.
Ardenhale consolidated gradually from a scatter of early settlements into its current four principal cities, a process that took generations and was never fully peaceful.
Ardenhale's most persistent internal conflict centers on an old unpaid blood-debt, a dispute old enough that few remember exactly how it started but recent enough that it still shapes local politics.

sections.title: Factions
paragraphs: A faction within Ardenhale actively contests grazing land, organizing support in whichever of the nation's cities gives it the most leverage.
This faction's central aim is control over a border shrine both sides claim, pursued through both legitimate political pressure and, when that fails, quieter means.
Its influence is concentrated in one or two of Ardenhale's four cities rather than spread evenly across the nation, which is exactly why the formal government has been slow to move against it.

A hereditary court balanced by a chartered merchant assembly remains this faction's chief opponent, treating it as a persistent irritant rather than an existential threat — a judgment that may not age well.

sections.title: Urban Life
paragraphs: Brackgate runs on guild rank determining status more than birth, a structure visible in everything from who sits closest to the governor at public gatherings to who gets first pick of goods at market.
Status in Brackgate runs on guild rank determining status more than birth, a system locals mostly accept as fair and outsiders mostly find baffling.
Brackgate's daily rhythm is set by communal meals at the clan-hall, observed closely enough that a stranger who ignores it draws immediate notice.
Brackgate is built from terraced stone built into the hillside, a style shaped directly by Kelmoria's climate and the materials its Human founders had on hand.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Brackgate answers upward to Ardenhale, governed by a hereditary court balanced by a chartered merchant assembly, though in practice its local rulers exercise considerable day-to-day discretion so long as tribute and trade flow as expected.
Formal authority in Brackgate rests with a local governor, confirmed by Ardenhale's central government but drawn, by long custom, from the city's own leading families.

Beneath the formal government, a network of informants loyal to a single retired spymaster exercises real influence in Brackgate — acknowledged quietly by everyone who actually has to get business done there.

Day-to-day administration in Brackgate runs through clan-appointed reeves who answer to their own elders first, a system that works well enough in ordinary times but strains badly under any real crisis.

sections.title: Tension
paragraphs: Brackgate's deepest ongoing friction is over control of a trade toll, a dispute that shapes local politics more than any formal law does.
Tension in Brackgate currently sits at a simmer — real, openly discussed, but not yet at open conflict.
The root of Brackgate's trouble is control of a trade toll, a dispute old enough that most residents have simply learned to live around it.
Brackgate rarely sees real violence over this, but trade disputes have been known to bring things close to a boil, especially during the busy trading season.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Brackgate was settled by Human migrants and grew into its current standing as a city on the strength of its trade in grain, which remains the backbone of its economy today.
Brackgate was founded by early Human settlers of Ardenhale, drawn to the site by exactly the resources that still support the city's trade.
In its history, Brackgate absorbed a wave of refugees who reshaped its culture within two generations, an event still referenced in local memory and civic ritual.
As a result, its founding event is reenacted every year as a public festival, a legacy every resident of Brackgate would recognize immediately even if outsiders rarely do.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Faerholt March is governed by an elected assembly of river-town delegates, an arrangement that grew directly out of how Half-Elf settlers on Kelmoria organized themselves in the generations after the Doubling of Founding. It has held largely unchanged since, adjusted at the margins but never formally overthrown.

Law in Faerholt March is set and interpreted by an elected assembly of river-town delegates, with each of the nation's four cities left to handle enforcement details locally so long as they don't contradict the nation's core code.
Authority in Faerholt March flows downward from an elected assembly of river-town delegates to each city's local ruler, who in turn answers for their city's conduct at the nation's periodic councils.

Faerholt March relies on city militias for day-to-day order, backed by standing patrols along its more contested borders — a compromise that keeps costs down but leaves remote stretches thinly watched.

sections.title: Identity
paragraphs: Faerholt March is a Half-Elf-majority nation on Kelmoria, and its laws, holidays, and public architecture all reflect Half-Elf custom even where other peoples make up a sizable minority of its population.

Faerholt March's stated priorities are preserving its autonomy, keeping its trade routes secure, and honoring the Long Peace Accords — though in practice the first two frequently take precedence over the third when they conflict.

Faerholt March occupies territory on Kelmoria that its people have held since before the Long Peace, giving its claim to the land a legitimacy few neighbors formally dispute, whatever they say in private.
Faerholt March maintains formal ties with its neighbors on Kelmoria and trade contacts reaching all three other continents, conducted mostly through its merchant houses rather than formal embassies.

sections.title: Economy
paragraphs: Faerholt March's economy runs on river tolls, ferried cargo, and mixed farmland produce, produced and traded through its four principal cities and shaping nearly every other aspect of its politics, from tax policy to who holds real influence in an elected assembly of river-town delegates.

Faerholt March produces river tolls, ferried cargo, and mixed farmland produce in quantities enough to export widely, a trade that has made certain families and guilds within the nation disproportionately wealthy and influential.

Faerholt March exports river tolls, ferried cargo, and mixed farmland produce through its four principal cities, trading them for goods its own land and craft cannot supply — a dependency that keeps its merchant houses politically powerful.

Labor in Faerholt March splits between guild-apprenticed craft work in its cities and traditional household or clan labor in its more rural stretches, with real tension between the two systems over status and pay.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Faerholt March was founded in the generations following the Doubling of Founding by Half-Elf settlers on Kelmoria, consolidating slowly from scattered early settlements into the nation recognized today.

Faerholt March's founding myths center on the Doubling of Founding and the nation's first recognized leader, whose exact deeds vary considerably depending on which city's version of the story is being told.
Faerholt March consolidated gradually from a scatter of early settlements into its current four principal cities, a process that took generations and was never fully peaceful.

Faerholt March's most persistent internal conflict centers on a border shrine both sides claim, a dispute old enough that few remember exactly how it started but recent enough that it still shapes local politics.

sections.title: Factions
paragraphs: A faction within Faerholt March actively contests grazing land, organizing support in whichever of the nation's cities gives it the most leverage.
This faction's central aim is control over an old unpaid blood-debt, pursued through both legitimate political pressure and, when that fails, quieter means.
Its influence is concentrated in one or two of Faerholt March's four cities rather than spread evenly across the nation, which is exactly why the formal government has been slow to move against it.
An elected assembly of river-town delegates remains this faction's chief opponent, treating it as a persistent irritant rather than an existential threat — a judgment that may not age well.

sections.title: Urban Life
paragraphs: Caelholt runs on a warrior caste ranked above artisans and laborers, a structure visible in everything from who sits closest to the reeve at public gatherings to who gets first pick of goods at market.
Status in Caelholt runs on a warrior caste ranked above artisans and laborers, a system locals mostly accept as fair and outsiders mostly find baffling.
Caelholt's daily rhythm is set by a dawn bell that opens the markets, observed closely enough that a stranger who ignores it draws immediate notice.
Caelholt is built from brick tenements stacked along a canal, a style shaped directly by Kelmoria's climate and the materials its Half-Elf founders had on hand.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Caelholt answers upward to Faerholt March, governed by an elected assembly of river-town delegates, though in practice its local rulers exercise considerable day-to-day discretion so long as tribute and trade flow as expected.
Formal authority in Caelholt rests with a local reeve, confirmed by Faerholt March's central government but drawn, by long custom, from the city's own leading families.

Beneath the formal government, a network of informants loyal to a single retired spymaster exercises real influence in Caelholt — acknowledged quietly by everyone who actually has to get business done there.
Day-to-day administration in Caelholt runs through a corps of literate scribes trained by the temple, a system that works well enough in ordinary times but strains badly under any real crisis.

sections.title: Tension
paragraphs: Caelholt's deepest ongoing friction is over smuggling routes, a dispute that shapes local politics more than any formal law does.
Tension in Caelholt currently sits at a simmer — real, openly discussed, but not yet at open conflict.
The root of Caelholt's trouble is smuggling routes, a dispute old enough that most residents have simply learned to live around it.
Caelholt rarely sees real violence over this, but trade disputes have been known to bring things close to a boil, especially during the busy trading season.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Caelholt was settled by Half-Elf migrants and grew into its current standing as a town on the strength of its trade in ferried cargo, which remains the backbone of its economy today.
Caelholt was founded by early Half-Elf settlers of Faerholt March, drawn to the site by exactly the resources that still support the city's trade.
In its history, Caelholt split from a larger settlement after a succession dispute, an event still referenced in local memory and civic ritual.
As a result, its founding compromise is still cited in local law, a legacy every resident of Caelholt would recognize immediately even if outsiders rarely do.

sections.title: Urban Life
paragraphs: Dunvale runs on a landed gentry above a tenant-farming majority, a structure visible in everything from who sits closest to the reeve at public gatherings to who gets first pick of goods at market.
Status in Dunvale runs on a landed gentry above a tenant-farming majority, a system locals mostly accept as fair and outsiders mostly find baffling.
Dunvale's daily rhythm is set by mandatory tithe-days each new moon, observed closely enough that a stranger who ignores it draws immediate notice.
Dunvale is built from sunken courtyard houses that trap the cool night air, a style shaped directly by Kelmoria's climate and the materials its Half-Elf founders had on hand.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Dunvale answers upward to Faerholt March, governed by an elected assembly of river-town delegates, though in practice its local rulers exercise considerable day-to-day discretion so long as tribute and trade flow as expected.
Formal authority in Dunvale rests with a local reeve, confirmed by Faerholt March's central government but drawn, by long custom, from the city's own leading families.

Beneath the formal government, a temple faction that quietly funds half the city guard's wages exercises real influence in Dunvale — acknowledged quietly by everyone who actually has to get business done there.
Day-to-day administration in Dunvale runs through a standing bureaucracy inherited from an older empire, a system that works well enough in ordinary times but strains badly under any real crisis.

sections.title: Tension
paragraphs: Dunvale's deepest ongoing friction is over a border shrine both sides claim, a dispute that shapes local politics more than any formal law does.
Tension in Dunvale currently sits at a simmer — real, openly discussed, but not yet at open conflict.
The root of Dunvale's trouble is a border shrine both sides claim, a dispute old enough that most residents have simply learned to live around it.
Dunvale rarely sees real violence over this, but trade disputes have been known to bring things close to a boil, especially during the busy trading season.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Dunvale was settled by Half-Elf migrants and grew into its current standing as a town on the strength of its trade in mixed farmland produce, which remains the backbone of its economy today.
Dunvale was founded by early Half-Elf settlers of Faerholt March, drawn to the site by exactly the resources that still support the city's trade.
In its history, Dunvale was founded explicitly to guard a mountain pass or river ford, an event still referenced in local memory and civic ritual.
As a result, its old founding families still hold outsized influence, a legacy every resident of Dunvale would recognize immediately even if outsiders rarely do.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Sylvaeth is governed by a council of elders drawn from the oldest forest-households, an arrangement that grew directly out of how Elf settlers on Kelmoria organized themselves in the generations after the Doubling of Founding. It has held largely unchanged since, adjusted at the margins but never formally overthrown.

Law in Sylvaeth is set and interpreted by a council of elders drawn from the oldest forest-households, with each of the nation's four cities left to handle enforcement details locally so long as they don't contradict the nation's core code.

Authority in Sylvaeth flows downward from a council of elders drawn from the oldest forest-households to each city's local ruler, who in turn answers for their city's conduct at the nation's periodic councils.
Sylvaeth relies on city militias for day-to-day order, backed by standing patrols along its more contested borders — a compromise that keeps costs down but leaves remote stretches thinly watched.

sections.title: Identity
paragraphs: Sylvaeth is a Elf-majority nation on Kelmoria, and its laws, holidays, and public architecture all reflect Elf custom even where other peoples make up a sizable minority of its population.

Sylvaeth's stated priorities are preserving its autonomy, keeping its trade routes secure, and honoring the Long Peace Accords — though in practice the first two frequently take precedence over the third when they conflict.
Sylvaeth occupies territory on Kelmoria that its people have held since before the Long Peace, giving its claim to the land a legitimacy few neighbors formally dispute, whatever they say in private.
Sylvaeth maintains formal ties with its neighbors on Kelmoria and trade contacts reaching all three other continents, conducted mostly through its merchant houses rather than formal embassies.

sections.title: Economy
paragraphs: Sylvaeth's economy runs on worked hardwood, preserved forest herbs, and fine crafted goods, produced and traded through its four principal cities and shaping nearly every other aspect of its politics, from tax policy to who holds real influence in a council of elders drawn from the oldest forest-households.

Sylvaeth produces worked hardwood, preserved forest herbs, and fine crafted goods in quantities enough to export widely, a trade that has made certain families and guilds within the nation disproportionately wealthy and influential.

Sylvaeth exports worked hardwood, preserved forest herbs, and fine crafted goods through its four principal cities, trading them for goods its own land and craft cannot supply — a dependency that keeps its merchant houses politically powerful.

Labor in Sylvaeth splits between guild-apprenticed craft work in its cities and traditional household or clan labor in its more rural stretches, with real tension between the two systems over status and pay.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Sylvaeth was founded in the generations following the Doubling of Founding by Elf settlers on Kelmoria, consolidating slowly from scattered early settlements into the nation recognized today.

Sylvaeth's founding myths center on the Doubling of Founding and the nation's first recognized leader, whose exact deeds vary considerably depending on which city's version of the story is being told.
Sylvaeth consolidated gradually from a scatter of early settlements into its current four principal cities, a process that took generations and was never fully peaceful.
Sylvaeth's most persistent internal conflict centers on a disputed succession, a dispute old enough that few remember exactly how it started but recent enough that it still shapes local politics.

sections.title: Factions
paragraphs: A faction within Sylvaeth actively contests smuggling routes, organizing support in whichever of the nation's cities gives it the most leverage.
This faction's central aim is control over a border shrine both sides claim, pursued through both legitimate political pressure and, when that fails, quieter means.
Its influence is concentrated in one or two of Sylvaeth's four cities rather than spread evenly across the nation, which is exactly why the formal government has been slow to move against it.

A council of elders drawn from the oldest forest-households remains this faction's chief opponent, treating it as a persistent irritant rather than an existential threat — a judgment that may not age well.

sections.title: Urban Life
paragraphs: Lorwood runs on guild rank determining status more than birth, a structure visible in everything from who sits closest to the governor at public gatherings to who gets first pick of goods at market.
Status in Lorwood runs on guild rank determining status more than birth, a system locals mostly accept as fair and outsiders mostly find baffling.
Lorwood's daily rhythm is set by a weekly rest-day observed even by the guard, observed closely enough that a stranger who ignores it draws immediate notice.
Lorwood is built from terraced stone built into the hillside, a style shaped directly by Kelmoria's climate and the materials its Elf founders had on hand.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Lorwood answers upward to Sylvaeth, governed by a council of elders drawn from the oldest forest-households, though in practice its local rulers exercise considerable day-to-day discretion so long as tribute and trade flow as expected.
Formal authority in Lorwood rests with a local governor, confirmed by Sylvaeth's central government but drawn, by long custom, from the city's own leading families.
Beneath the formal government, an old veterans' league nobody in office will cross exercises real influence in Lorwood — acknowledged quietly by everyone who actually has to get business done there.

Day-to-day administration in Lorwood runs through clan-appointed reeves who answer to their own elders first, a system that works well enough in ordinary times but strains badly under any real crisis.

sections.title: Tension
paragraphs: Lorwood's deepest ongoing friction is over control of a trade toll, a dispute that shapes local politics more than any formal law does.
Tension in Lorwood currently sits at a simmer — real, openly discussed, but not yet at open conflict.
The root of Lorwood's trouble is control of a trade toll, a dispute old enough that most residents have simply learned to live around it.
Lorwood rarely sees real violence over this, but trade disputes have been known to bring things close to a boil, especially during the busy trading season.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Lorwood was settled by Elf migrants and grew into its current standing as a city on the strength of its trade in worked hardwood, which remains the backbone of its economy today.
Lorwood was founded by early Elf settlers of Sylvaeth, drawn to the site by exactly the resources that still support the city's trade.
In its history, Lorwood burned once, entirely, and was rebuilt on the same foundations out of stubbornness, an event still referenced in local memory and civic ritual.
As a result, outsiders still call it by its older, pre-founding name, a legacy every resident of Lorwood would recognize immediately even if outsiders rarely do.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Tinkerhome Delve is governed by a guild consortium that rotates its chair every season, an arrangement that grew directly out of how Gnome settlers on Kelmoria organized themselves in the generations after the Doubling of Founding. It has held largely unchanged since, adjusted at the margins but never formally overthrown.

Law in Tinkerhome Delve is set and interpreted by a guild consortium that rotates its chair every season, with each of the nation's four cities left to handle enforcement details locally so long as they don't contradict the nation's core code.

Authority in Tinkerhome Delve flows downward from a guild consortium that rotates its chair every season to each city's local ruler, who in turn answers for their city's conduct at the nation's periodic councils.

Tinkerhome Delve relies on city militias for day-to-day order, backed by standing patrols along its more contested borders — a compromise that keeps costs down but leaves remote stretches thinly watched.

sections.title: Identity
paragraphs: Tinkerhome Delve is a Gnome-majority nation on Kelmoria, and its laws, holidays, and public architecture all reflect Gnome custom even where other peoples make up a sizable minority of its population.

Tinkerhome Delve's stated priorities are preserving its autonomy, keeping its trade routes secure, and honoring the Long Peace Accords — though in practice the first two frequently take precedence over the third when they conflict.

Tinkerhome Delve occupies territory on Kelmoria that its people have held since before the Long Peace, giving its claim to the land a legitimacy few neighbors formally dispute, whatever they say in private.

Tinkerhome Delve maintains formal ties with its neighbors on Kelmoria and trade contacts reaching all three other continents, conducted mostly through its merchant houses rather than formal embassies.

sections.title: Economy
paragraphs: Tinkerhome Delve's economy runs on clockwork devices, alchemical curiosities, and novelty trade goods, produced and traded through its four principal cities and shaping nearly every other aspect of its politics, from tax policy to who holds real influence in a guild consortium that rotates its chair every season.

Tinkerhome Delve produces clockwork devices, alchemical curiosities, and novelty trade goods in quantities enough to export widely, a trade that has made certain families and guilds within the nation disproportionately wealthy and influential.

Tinkerhome Delve exports clockwork devices, alchemical curiosities, and novelty trade goods through its four principal cities, trading them for goods its own land and craft cannot supply — a dependency that keeps its merchant houses politically powerful.

Labor in Tinkerhome Delve splits between guild-apprenticed craft work in its cities and traditional household or clan labor in its more rural stretches, with real tension between the two systems over status and pay.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Tinkerhome Delve was founded in the generations following the Doubling of Founding by Gnome settlers on Kelmoria, consolidating slowly from scattered early settlements into the nation recognized today.

Tinkerhome Delve's founding myths center on the Doubling of Founding and the nation's first recognized leader, whose exact deeds vary considerably depending on which city's version of the story is being told.
Tinkerhome Delve consolidated gradually from a scatter of early settlements into its current four principal cities, a process that took generations and was never fully peaceful.

Tinkerhome Delve's most persistent internal conflict centers on a disputed succession, a dispute old enough that few remember exactly how it started but recent enough that it still shapes local politics.

sections.title: Factions
paragraphs: A faction within Tinkerhome Delve actively contests smuggling routes, organizing support in whichever of the nation's cities gives it the most leverage.
This faction's central aim is control over a border shrine both sides claim, pursued through both legitimate political pressure and, when that fails, quieter means.
Its influence is concentrated in one or two of Tinkerhome Delve's four cities rather than spread evenly across the nation, which is exactly why the formal government has been slow to move against it.

A guild consortium that rotates its chair every season remains this faction's chief opponent, treating it as a persistent irritant rather than an existential threat — a judgment that may not age well.

sections.title: Urban Life
paragraphs: Brixwick runs on clan seniority set by age and deed, a structure visible in everything from who sits closest to the governor at public gatherings to who gets first pick of goods at market.
Status in Brixwick runs on clan seniority set by age and deed, a system locals mostly accept as fair and outsiders mostly find baffling.
Brixwick's daily rhythm is set by ritual bathing before any formal business, observed closely enough that a stranger who ignores it draws immediate notice.
Brixwick is built from black basalt blockhouses with narrow windows, a style shaped directly by Kelmoria's climate and the materials its Gnome founders had on hand.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Brixwick answers upward to Tinkerhome Delve, governed by a guild consortium that rotates its chair every season, though in practice its local rulers exercise considerable day-to-day discretion so long as tribute and trade flow as expected.
Formal authority in Brixwick rests with a local governor, confirmed by Tinkerhome Delve's central government but drawn, by long custom, from the city's own leading families.
Beneath the formal government, a black-market alchemist collective exercises real influence in Brixwick — acknowledged quietly by everyone who actually has to get business done there.
Day-to-day administration in Brixwick runs through tax-farmers who keep a cut of everything they collect, a system that works well enough in ordinary times but strains badly under any real crisis.

sections.title: Tension
paragraphs: Brixwick's deepest ongoing friction is over a heretical splinter cult, a dispute that shapes local politics more than any formal law does.
Tension in Brixwick currently sits at a simmer — real, openly discussed, but not yet at open conflict.
The root of Brixwick's trouble is a heretical splinter cult, a dispute old enough that most residents have simply learned to live around it.
Brixwick rarely sees real violence over this, but trade disputes have been known to bring things close to a boil, especially during the busy trading season.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Brixwick was settled by Gnome migrants and grew into its current standing as a city on the strength of its trade in clockwork devices, which remains the backbone of its economy today.
Brixwick was founded by early Gnome settlers of Tinkerhome Delve, drawn to the site by exactly the resources that still support the city's trade.
In its history, Brixwick was founded explicitly to guard a mountain pass or river ford, an event still referenced in local memory and civic ritual.
As a result, outsiders still call it by its older, pre-founding name, a legacy every resident of Brixwick would recognize immediately even if outsiders rarely do.

sections.title: Urban Life
paragraphs: Sparburrow runs on a landed gentry above a tenant-farming majority, a structure visible in everything from who sits closest to the reeve at public gatherings to who gets first pick of goods at market.
Status in Sparburrow runs on a landed gentry above a tenant-farming majority, a system locals mostly accept as fair and outsiders mostly find baffling.
Sparburrow's daily rhythm is set by a dusk curfew for the unescorted young, observed closely enough that a stranger who ignores it draws immediate notice.
Sparburrow is built from black basalt blockhouses with narrow windows, a style shaped directly by Kelmoria's climate and the materials its Gnome founders had on hand.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Sparburrow answers upward to Tinkerhome Delve, governed by a guild consortium that rotates its chair every season, though in practice its local rulers exercise considerable day-to-day discretion so long as tribute and trade flow as expected.
Formal authority in Sparburrow rests with a local reeve, confirmed by Tinkerhome Delve's central government but drawn, by long custom, from the city's own leading families.

Beneath the formal government, a temple faction that quietly funds half the city guard's wages exercises real influence in Sparburrow — acknowledged quietly by everyone who actually has to get business done there.
Day-to-day administration in Sparburrow runs through tax-farmers who keep a cut of everything they collect, a system that works well enough in ordinary times but strains badly under any real crisis.

sections.title: Tension
paragraphs: Sparburrow's deepest ongoing friction is over a heretical splinter cult, a dispute that shapes local politics more than any formal law does.
Tension in Sparburrow currently sits at a simmer — real, openly discussed, but not yet at open conflict.
The root of Sparburrow's trouble is a heretical splinter cult, a dispute old enough that most residents have simply learned to live around it.
Sparburrow rarely sees real violence over this, but trade disputes have been known to bring things close to a boil, especially during the busy trading season.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Sparburrow was settled by Gnome migrants and grew into its current standing as a town on the strength of its trade in alchemical curiosities, which remains the backbone of its economy today.
Sparburrow was founded by early Gnome settlers of Tinkerhome Delve, drawn to the site by exactly the resources that still support the city's trade.
In its history, Sparburrow survived a siege that the founding generation still tells stories about, an event still referenced in local memory and civic ritual.
As a result, it is now the region's acknowledged center of learning, a legacy every resident of Sparburrow would recognize immediately even if outsiders rarely do.

sections.title: Geography
paragraphs: Sunkeep Reaches is defined by high desert plateau, undercliff cave networks, scattered oases — a landscape that shaped every nation built on it long before any of their current borders existed. A long mountain spine with deep hold-riddled roots, dry plateau to the east sets the pattern of where people actually settled, and the climate — hot days, cold nights, rare but violent seasonal storms — decided what they could grow, mine, or hunt once they did.

The mix of high desert plateau, undercliff cave networks, scattered oases on Sunkeep Reaches means no single nation here can rely on one kind of land; every nation's economy blends what each biome offers rather than specializing in just one.

A long mountain spine with deep hold-riddled roots, dry plateau to the east across Sunkeep Reaches has kept its four nations more separated by geography than by any deliberate border policy — most conflicts here start at a natural chokepoint, not an arbitrary line.

A hot days, cold nights, rare but violent seasonal storms climate governs the planting, trading, and travel calendar for every nation on Sunkeep Reaches, and every one of them has built its major festivals around it.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Sunkeep Reaches has been settled continuously since before the Doubling of Founding, first by scattered clans of its founding peoples and later by the four organized nations that now hold it. The Veil-Storms of -410 reshaped its coastline and interior alike, and the Long Peace Accords of 112 are still the framework every nation here formally honors, however unevenly.
Histories on Sunkeep Reaches are conventionally divided into the Founding Era (before -410), the unstable Veil-Storm centuries that followed, and the Long Peace that has held, roughly, since 112.
The Veil-Storms remain the single most-referenced disaster in every nation's oldest records on Sunkeep Reaches, blamed for everything from reshaped coastlines to the continent's scattered wild zones.

Population on Sunkeep Reaches has drifted steadily toward its rivers, coasts, and trade roads for generations, hollowing out its more remote interior settlements in favor of its four nations' capitals and market towns.

sections.title: Demographics
paragraphs: Sunkeep Reaches is home to the Dwarf, Halfling, Ratfolk, Tengu peoples, each concentrated in its own nation but present as trading minorities nearly everywhere else on the continent.
Dwarf, Halfling, Ratfolk, Tengu together make up the overwhelming majority of Sunkeep Reaches's population, with small numbers of other Aurvantan peoples present in every major port and market town.

Movement across Sunkeep Reaches runs mostly along its trade roads and river lines rather than across open wilderness, which keeps its nations' borders porous for merchants even when politically tense.
Sunkeep Reaches supports a population in the low millions, weighted heavily toward its four national capitals and the market towns strung along the routes between them.

sections.title: Governance
paragraphs: Kharzun Delve is governed by clan-king holds bound by an ancient mutual-defense oath, an arrangement that grew directly out of how Dwarf settlers on Sunkeep Reaches organized themselves in the generations after the Doubling of Founding. It has held largely unchanged since, adjusted at the margins but never formally overthrown.

Law in Kharzun Delve is set and interpreted by clan-king holds bound by an ancient mutual-defense oath, with each of the nation's four cities left to handle enforcement details locally so long as they don't contradict the nation's core code.

Authority in Kharzun Delve flows downward from clan-king holds bound by an ancient mutual-defense oath to each city's local ruler, who in turn answers for their city's conduct at the nation's periodic councils.

Kharzun Delve relies on city militias for day-to-day order, backed by standing patrols along its more contested borders — a compromise that keeps costs down but leaves remote stretches thinly watched.

sections.title: Identity
paragraphs: Kharzun Delve is a Dwarf-majority nation on Sunkeep Reaches, and its laws, holidays, and public architecture all reflect Dwarf custom even where other peoples make up a sizable minority of its population.

Kharzun Delve's stated priorities are preserving its autonomy, keeping its trade routes secure, and honoring the Long Peace Accords — though in practice the first two frequently take precedence over the third when they conflict.

Kharzun Delve occupies territory on Sunkeep Reaches that its people have held since before the Long Peace, giving its claim to the land a legitimacy few neighbors formally dispute, whatever they say in private.

Kharzun Delve maintains formal ties with its neighbors on Sunkeep Reaches and trade contacts reaching all three other continents, conducted mostly through its merchant houses rather than formal embassies.

sections.title: Economy
paragraphs: Kharzun Delve's economy runs on gemstones, worked metal, and deep-mined ore, produced and traded through its four principal cities and shaping nearly every other aspect of its politics, from tax policy to who holds real influence in clan-king holds bound by an ancient mutual-defense oath.

Kharzun Delve produces gemstones, worked metal, and deep-mined ore in quantities enough to export widely, a trade that has made certain families and guilds within the nation disproportionately wealthy and influential.

Kharzun Delve exports gemstones, worked metal, and deep-mined ore through its four principal cities, trading them for goods its own land and craft cannot supply — a dependency that keeps its merchant houses politically powerful.

Labor in Kharzun Delve splits between guild-apprenticed craft work in its cities and traditional household or clan labor in its more rural stretches, with real tension between the two systems over status and pay.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: Kharzun Delve was founded in the generations following the Doubling of Founding by Dwarf settlers on Sunkeep Reaches, consolidating slowly from scattered early settlements into the nation recognized today.

Kharzun Delve's founding myths center on the Doubling of Founding and the nation's first recognized leader, whose exact deeds vary considerably depending on which city's version of the story is being told.
Kharzun Delve consolidated gradually from a scatter of early settlements into its current four principal cities, a process that took generations and was never fully peaceful.

Kharzun Delve's most persistent internal conflict centers on control of a trade toll, a dispute old enough that few remember exactly how it started but recent enough that it still shapes local politics.

sections.title: Factions
paragraphs: A faction within Kharzun Delve actively contests an old unpaid blood-debt, organizing support in whichever of the nation's cities gives it the most leverage.
This faction's central aim is control over grazing land, pursued through both legitimate political pressure and, when that fails, quieter means.
Its influence is concentrated in one or two of Kharzun Delve's four cities rather than spread evenly across the nation, which is exactly why the formal government has been slow to move against it.

Clan-king holds bound by an ancient mutual-defense oath remains this faction's chief opponent, treating it as a persistent irritant rather than an existential threat — a judgment that may not age well.
